title: Robot vacuum: safe teardown
summary: A robot vacuum gives a 14.4 V battery pack, two geared wheel modules, brush and fan motors, infrared cliff and bump sensors, a main board and a mains charging dock. The pack is the main danger. Take it out first, before you touch the brushes, which can start without warning while it is in.

steps.text: Before you charge it or open it, put it on a bench outdoors, right way up, and look it over without touching its buttons or brushes: cracks, a bulging battery door, scorch marks, melted plastic, leaks, heat or a sweet chemical smell. If you find any of these, don't charge it and don't put it on its dock: follow safety_swollen_lithium. Never charge a damaged or leaking pack (Roomba 600 guide).
steps.warn: Shorting a robot's battery terminals can cause burns or a fire, and liquid from a damaged pack can irritate or burn skin and eyes (Roborock S7 manual).

steps.text: Switch the robot off with its button, lift it off the dock, and unplug the dock from the wall.
steps.warn: The Roborock S7 manual warns that the main brush may start unexpectedly and says to disconnect it before cleaning or servicing. Keep fingers off the brushes until the battery is out.

steps.text: Turn the robot over on a soft cloth and don't press its buttons. Get the battery out before you touch the main brush or the wheels. The Roomba 560, 655 and 890 and the Roborock S5 Max and S7 guides take the side brush off first (iFixit Roomba 560 battery, iFixit Roomba 655 brush motor, iFixit Roomba 890 wheel, iFixit S5 Max, iFixit S7); the Roomba 980 guide goes straight to the back plate (iFixit Roomba 980 battery): if it blocks the pack, hold the robot still, touch only the brush's screw and hub, never its bristles, and take the pack out straight after. Roombas: undo the back-plate screws, then lift the pack by its pull tabs (iFixit Roomba 980 battery, iFixit Roomba 560 battery). Roborock: take off the side brush and the bottom panel, lift the pack out, then squeeze its connector to release it (iFixit S5 Max, iFixit S7).
steps.warn: Release the connector by its body, not the cable. Yanking can tear it off the main board (iFixit S5 Max). Tape over both halves.

steps.text: Look at the pack now it is out. Swollen, dented, leaking, hot or smelly means stop and follow safety_swollen_lithium. Read its label for the chemistry: lithium-ion (Li-ion) or nickel-metal hydride (NiMH). Tape over its contacts and keep it whole: iRobot says not to crush or take packs apart (Roomba 600 guide).
Outdoors, with a dust mask on, empty the dust bin into a bag and take out its filter. Seal the bag.

Pull off the main brushes and side brush, then open the top: the Roborock S7's cover comes off on latches and screws, and the Roomba 581's faceplate unclips with a spudger (iFixit S7, iFixit Roomba 581).
LiDAR robots: take the rubber caps off the cage screws, undo them and lift off the cage, then undo the LiDAR's own screws and lift the turret out whole (iFixit S7, iFixit S5 Max).
steps.warn: The turret holds a laser: the S7 manual carries a laser safety notice (Roborock S7 manual). Keep the turret closed and don't look into it while it runs.

steps.text: Undo the bumper and chassis screws. Unplug the bumper's sensor wires at the main board before you pull the bumper away (iFixit Roomba 581).
Unplug the main board's connectors, undo its screws and tilt it out rather than lifting it straight up (iFixit Roomba 581).
steps.warn: Don't bend the parts round the board: on the Roomba 581, MOSFET heat sinks that touch can short (iFixit Roomba 581).

steps.text: Undo the wheel module's screws and pull it out; how it fastens varies by model, so check yours. Keep it whole as a geared drive. To open one, take its shock spring off first, as the guide does, so the wheel can't jump off (the guide gives no details of how), then push out the pivot pin and undo the housing screws to free the motor and gears (iFixit Roomba 650 wheel).
steps.warn: The shock spring is small but loaded. Hold the wheel while you unhook it, and wear glasses.

steps.text: Unscrew the brush motor and side-brush motor from the cleaning head. Where the leads are soldered, as on the Roomba 655, don't pull them: the guide warns a hard pull can snap a wire. Cut them one at a time near the motor, with the battery still out (iFixit Roomba 655 brush motor).
Lift out the vacuum fan as one unit with its housing. On the Roomba 560 the motor and housing come out together, and repairing the fan itself would need soldering (iFixit Roomba 560 fan).
Take the cliff sensors (they clip into the chassis), the bump switches, the infrared bumper sensor, the speaker, the DC jack and the charging contacts (iFixit Roomba 581).

Keep the dock closed if you can. It is a mains power supply: the Roborock S7's takes 100–240 V AC (Roborock S7 manual), and iRobot says the Roomba Home Base has no user-serviceable parts (Roomba 600 guide). To open it, follow safety_mains_isolation. Take the robot off the dock. Pull the plug at the outlet, or at the UPS or inverter it runs from, and keep it in sight. Wait 5 minutes, then open the case. Discharge the largest capacitor with a resistor tool (safety_discharge_capacitor). Prove the dock dead at the capacitor and the wires you will touch, with a meter you have checked on a known source, and check the meter on that source again afterwards. It must read under 1 V: leave a wire across the capacitor while you work.
steps.warn: Never open the dock while it is plugged in. A power supply's capacitor can hold a charge after unplugging: discharge it and prove it dead before you touch it. Keep the robot off the dock so no battery touches its contacts (Roomba 600 guide).

notes:
## What's worth keeping and why

- **Battery pack.** The Roomba 600 series takes a NiMH pack of up to 3000 mAh or a Li-ion pack of up to 3300 mAh, 14.8 V at most (Roomba 600 guide). The Roborock S7 uses a lithium-ion pack (Roborock S7 manual). A 14.4 V lithium-ion pack is four cells in series; a 14.4 V NiMH pack is twelve 1.2 V cells. Use the pack whole, through a fuse, for LED lights or a radio; give 12 V gear a DC-DC converter, because a full four-cell lithium-ion pack sits near 16.8 V. Charge it in its own robot on its own dock, or with a charger made for that chemistry: the Roborock manual says a charger made for one pack type can start a fire with another pack, and iRobot says other battery types than its listed ones may burst (Roborock S7 manual, Roomba 600 guide).
- **Wheel modules.** Each holds a small DC motor, a gear train and a shock spring (iFixit Roomba 650 wheel). Whole, a module is a ready-made slow geared drive for a small cart or robot, a turntable or a light winch. Run it at the pack's voltage or less.
- **Brush and side-brush motors.** Small DC motors. On the Roomba 655 the brush motor sits in the brush holder with its own small board (iFixit Roomba 655 brush motor).
- **Vacuum fan.** A small, fast blower: air for a small stove or a fume fan.
- **Sensors.** The Roomba 581 has cliff sensors, bump switches, an infrared bumper sensor and a caster detection piece with its own LEDs (iFixit Roomba 581). Use them as edge or obstacle detectors and door switches.
- **LiDAR turret.** A spinning laser range finder. Reusing it needs software for its data, so keep it whole. The S7 came with three different LiDAR versions (iFixit S7).
- **Main board.** Little use whole. Its MOSFETs are spares (iFixit Roomba 581).
- **Speaker, DC jack and charging contacts** (iFixit Roomba 581).
- **Dock.** A small mains power supply. The Roborock S7 dock takes 100–240 V AC and gives 20 V DC at 1.2 A (Roborock S7 manual). The Roomba Home Base is a dock with a built-in charger and no user-serviceable parts (Roomba 600 guide). Read the label on yours.

## Variations

- **Roomba 500 and 600:** modular. On the 581 the battery and the blue modules come out after 12 captive screws, and the main board sits under the chassis top. Its top port is a DIN-8 socket for add-on modules or reprogramming (iFixit Roomba 581). The 560's battery is under a four-screw back panel (iFixit Roomba 560 battery).
- **Roomba 980:** the battery is under a screwed-on back plate, after two more screws (iFixit Roomba 980 battery).
- **Roborock S5 Max and S7:** a LiDAR turret on top; the battery is under the bottom panel and its connector tears easily (iFixit S5 Max, iFixit S7).
- **Battery chemistry:** the Roomba 600 series could have either NiMH or Li-ion (Roomba 600 guide). Read the pack label.

## Battery and brush safety

- The S7's main brush may start without warning, and its manual says to disconnect it before cleaning or servicing (Roborock S7 manual). Keep your fingers off the main brush and wheels until the battery is out. If the side brush has to come off first to reach the battery, touch only its screw and hub.
- Shorting the battery terminals can cause burns or a fire. If liquid comes out of a pack and touches you, flush with water; if it gets in your eyes, get medical help as well (Roborock S7 manual).
- Check packs for damage or leaks before use. Don't charge a damaged or leaking pack, and don't crush or take one apart (Roomba 600 guide).
- Heat above 54 °C (130 °F) damages lithium cells, and so does charging below freezing (OSHA SHIB 06-20-2019). Store spare packs part-charged, terminals taped, in a metal box away from where people sleep (safety_swollen_lithium).

## What to leave

- **Swollen, leaking or damaged packs.** Store them in sand outdoors (safety_swollen_lithium).
- **The inside of the LiDAR turret.**
- **The inside of the dock,** unless you need its small power supply.
- **Old dust and filters.** They can hold mould.
- **The plastic shell, bumper and bin.**

## Testing what you got out

- **Pack:** measure DC volts at its contacts. A four-cell lithium-ion pack reads about 12–16.8 V. Much lower means flat or failing cells: don't charge it. For a NiMH pack, compare with its label.
- **Motors:** two-wire DC motors run briefly from a 12 V battery through a fuse. A wheel module should turn slowly and strongly (see test_motor).
